title: Latency/Throughput Oscillator: Smooth phase blending for prefill/decode
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: We see frequent mode oscillation at the per-GPU scheduler layer when tenant mix changes rapidly: the system flips between aggressive phase-splitting (throughput mode) and conservative single-phase routing (latency mode). This causes tail latency spikes and reduced steady-state throughput for mixed workloads.

Goal: Implement a 'Latency/Throughput Oscillator'—a smoothing controller that blends phase-splitting aggressiveness over a configurable time window using kernel latency probes and attention-sparsity indicators. The controller should reduce oscillation, preserve latency SLOs for latency-sensitive requests, and recover throughput for bulk decoding jobs without manual tier switching.

Design overview:
- Input signals: moving-window kernel latency percentiles (p50/p95), per-tenant microburst count, attention-sparsity score (from prefill analysis), and KV-cache hit ratio.
- Output: a continuous aggressiveness factor alpha in [0,1] where alpha=0 prefers low-latency single-phase routing and alpha=1 enables multi-phase splitting and opportunistic batching.
- Controller: a damped oscillator-style PID with two additions: (1) kernel-feedback damping term that scales with recent p95 delta, (2) 'grandfathering' for in-flight low-latency requests (requests already in decode path get protected for short window).
- Phase-splitting policy: map alpha to split granularity and maximum per-request concurrent slices. Use kernel hints to prefer slices that align with available fast kernels (8-bit matmul paths).

Trade-offs and decisions:
- We avoid hard binary mode switches; preference is for continuous blending to reduce churn in kernel allocation.
- Grandfathering increases short-term capacity usage but prevents latency regressions for active interactive sessions.
- Kernel-probing frequency must be bounded to avoid extra overhead; choose sampling every 250ms by default with adaptive backoff.

Acceptance criteria:
- On mixed synthetic workloads, 95th percentile latency for latency-sensitive class improves by >=20% vs current oscillating baseline while throughput drop for bulk jobs <=10% over 30-minute runs.
- No increase in GPU kernel launch errors or memory fragmentation in canary cluster.
- Controller exposes alpha and signal metrics to Console dashboards with 1s resolution.

Milestones:
1) 2025-02-20: Prototype controller + unit tests in scheduler repo (alpha toggled off by default).
2) 2025-02-27: Integration with kernel latency probes + offline simulation harness.
3) 2025-03-05: Canary rollout to dedicated pool (10% traffic) + dashboard.
4) 2025-03-15: Full rollout and postmortem.

Testing plan:
- Synthetic: mixed interactive 10 qps small sequences + bulk batch decode at 40 qps; run 1h with step changes in ratio to induce oscillation.
- Replay: use production trace replay from 2025-01-28 incident to validate no regression.
- Resource tests: ensure KV cache behaviour unchanged under alpha=1.

Rollout and observability:
- New Console metrics: scheduler.alpha, kernel_probe.p95, attn_sparsity.score, runway.grandfathered_count.
- Flags: runtime.scheduling.oscillator.enabled (false by default), runtime.scheduling.oscillator.window_ms, runtime.scheduling.oscillator.sampling_ms.

Links: Confluence design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/OSCILLATOR-2025, RFC PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/scheduler/pull/1234, simulation dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/oscillator-sim

Risks: controller mis-tuning can mask real capacity shortages; mitigate by circuit-breaker that disables optimistic splits when sustained p99 kernel latency > 3x baseline for 2 minutes.

Longer-term: integrate oscillator with tenant-weighted SLA signals so alpha can be nudged per-tenant rather than global pool-wide (follow-up ticket).
